evidence.finding: Routing version 24.7 was deployed across all queues at the 09:15 incident start.
Mean transfer rate rose 101.46%, from 6.2163% before the incident to 12.5234% afterward.
Mean AHT rose 35.04%, from 378.037 to 510.5161 seconds after incident onset.
Mean service level fell 19.8117 percentage points, from 80.7977% to 60.986%.
Observed offered calls declined 6.10% across the incident boundary, excluding an aggregate demand surge.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained at 49; productive staffing changed by only 0.68%.
Every queue experienced an approximately 35–38% AHT increase and 88–117% transfer-rate increase, while service-level severity varied by queue.

primary_root_cause_detail: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed across all queues at 09:15, exactly when transfer rates doubled and AHT increased roughly 35% across every queue. The added transfer and handling workload reduced throughput, increased ASA, and degraded service level despite stable staffing and flat-to-lower demand.
recommended_actions: Roll back or correct routing configuration version 24.7 and validate route and transfer rules before redeployment.
Monitor transfer rate, AHT, ASA, and service level by queue immediately after remediation.
Add predeployment tests for transfer loops, unintended queue hops, and queue-level routing outcomes.
Establish automated postdeployment alerts for abrupt transfer-rate and AHT changes.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Aggregate offered volume declined after incident onset, and no queue experienced a material demand surge.
Scheduled and logged-in headcount remained constant, with no material productive-staffing reduction.
Queue staffing was unchanged and the transfer/AHT shock affected every queue, indicating a system-wide routing effect rather than a localized capacity imbalance.
No platform event corroborated the degradation; the only contemporaneous operational event was the routing deployment.
The AHT increase was a material mechanism, but the exactly contemporaneous routing deployment and transfer-rate increase provide the deeper initiating cause.

stakeholder_summary: The service-level incident was most likely caused by routing version 24.7. Its deployment coincided exactly with system-wide increases in transfers and handling time, reducing throughput while demand and staffing remained stable.
